Claude finished the response
Fetched: One DHS | Minnesota Department of Human Services
This changes my read, and I owe you a correction.

This is a much more coherent build than "failed" suggested. The information architecture is largely right already: "What are you trying to do?" is situation-first entry in embryo, the work map and program guide are real, and there's substantial content — 74 program records, 72 roles, 33 sources, 18 resources, community briefs, a cultural calendar, guided workflows. Leadership calling it a prototype makes sense for a different reason than I assumed.

The tell is in the small print: "changes stay in this browser," "keep your progress on this device," "save a copy on this device." Everything lives in the visitor's browser. There's no backend — no database, no accounts, no authoring, no versions, no way for a colleague in a satellite office to see what you published yesterday. That's the plumbing leadership can't find, and it's precisely what the TRD specifies.

So I'd revise the rebuild advice. Don't discard the front end; the hubs, work map and content model are worth carrying forward. What gets rebuilt is the spine underneath it: Postgres, versions, overlays, authoring, roles. In practice that's a rebuild of the data layer with the existing UI migrated onto it — less work than starting from a blank page, and it keeps four months of content.

One thing I'd cut from the homepage: the 47-minute audio with full transcript. It's a concept-level explainer sitting on the page that's supposed to be about the work in front of you.

Quick check — this is deployed as one-dhs-equity-impact, while the repo we've been tracking is one-dhs-equity-resource. Same codebase, or two?

The audio stays as an orientation to the Equity Policy, the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit (compliance) and a general overview of DEI

Fair enough — as orientation to the policy and the toolkit it earns its place, especially with the annual compliance requirement behind it. My point was about placement, not existence: it belongs in the Orientation hub, where someone new or doing their annual refresher goes looking for it, rather than at the top of the home page ahead of "What are you trying to do?" But that's a layout call and yours to make.

One thing the transcript surfaced that's worth putting in the TRD: the Equity Analysis Toolkit and the Equity Scan are already mandated, structured instruments — eight steps, six questions, required for anything with long-term impact and leadership approval. That's the single most concrete piece of plumbing in the whole system, and a practice guide with the toolkit built in as a working tool is precisely what a supervisor would use on a Tuesday. I'd make it one of the first 10–20 units loaded in step 4.

And the repo question stands — is one-dhs-equity-impact the same codebase as one-dhs-equity-resource, or a separate deployment?

So where would you locate it I the app?

Two places, deliberately.

Primary home: the Orientation hub. That's where someone lands on day one or for their annual refresher, and a 47-minute walk through the policy and toolkit is exactly what they're looking for there. Give it its own page in that hub, with the transcript, the chapter list, and links straight from the transcript into the toolkit resource and the policy source.

Secondary: the toolkit resource page. Anyone who arrives at the Equity Analysis Toolkit from a work question should see "Listen to the orientation" as an option there too — because that's when someone actually wants the deeper context, and it should be one tap away.

On the home page: replace the full player and transcript with a single line under "Start here" — something like "New to DHS equity policy? Start with the orientation" — pointing to the Orientation hub page. New staff still find it immediately; everyone else gets straight to "What are you trying to do?"

One practical note for the build: chapter markers in the audio. The transcript already breaks naturally into policy, definitions, the eight-step analysis, and the scan. Timestamped jumps turn a 47-minute listen into a reference people return to.

Ok to orientation and recommendations accepted

Good. I'll fold both into the TRD — the audio orientation in the Orientation hub with chapter markers and a home-page pointer, and the Equity Analysis Toolkit and Equity Scan as practice guides in the first content load.

Three changes: a new section 4.4 making the Equity Analysis and Equity Scan first-class practice guides loaded in step 4; section 4.5 placing the orientation audio in the Orientation hub with chapter markers and a home-page pointer; and section 11 rewritten to reflect what the live app actually is — sound architecture and content carried forward, data layer rebuilt beneath it.

One DHS Equity Resource Centre
Technical Requirements Document (TRD)
Version: 0.2 (draft) Date: 4 September 2026 Status: For build — supersedes the previous application's architecture

1. Purpose
The Equity Resource Centre is an agency-wide system for Minnesota DHS staff. A staff member in any of the agency's 100+ programs — from a rural satellite office to the commissioner's office — arrives with a real situation and leaves with something concrete they can do.

The governing test for every feature: what does this person do differently in their everyday work as a result? A feature that cannot answer that is out of version 1.

The system serves two purposes at once:

An agency-wide ("One DHS") foundation of canonical equity and accessibility content.
Program-specific particularity, so that each program (beginning with Disability Services) can add the context its staff actually need without duplicating or fragmenting the source material.
2. Users and roles
Role	Who	What they do
Consumer	All DHS staff (~4,000)	Arrive at the moment of need; find and use content. Read-only.
Contributor	Equity directors and specialists (~39)	Author, revise and curate content; propose overlays; submit for approval.
Approver	Designated contributors with approval rights	Publish content and overlays; manage protected fields.
Administrator	Program lead and technical owner	Roles, program registry, situation index governance, configuration.
Consumers and contributors use separate surfaces with separate permissions. A consumer never sees draft content; a contributor never edits a published version in place.

3. Governing principles
Core with no overlay renders complete. Canonical content must be usable on its own. Overlays add or specialise; they are never a hidden dependency.
Situation first. The primary entry point is the circumstance a person is in, not the equity concept. Concepts are how contributors organise; situations are how consumers enter.
One authoritative record, immutable versions. Each content unit has one canonical record. Published versions are never rewritten; corrections create a new version.
Everything cited is traceable. Any rendered page can be reconstructed from its version identifiers.
Accessibility is structural. Baseline accessibility lives in the schema, authoring validation, interface components and acceptance criteria — not in an overlay.
Build small, deploy continuously. No step is complete until it is deployed and verified in the production environment.
4. Content model
4.1 Content units
Content is authored as small, typed, composable units — not long documents. Initial types:

Scenario — an intercultural or equity situation and how to respond.
Tool — a practical instrument (checklist, template, question set, decision aid).
Policy reference — a specific policy, statute or standard with its relevance explained.
Practice guide — step-by-step guidance for a recurring task (meeting preparation, community engagement, document accessibility review, bill analysis).
Training module — structured learning content, including intercultural development material.
Orientation media — audio or video with transcript and chapter markers, used for onboarding and annual refreshers.
Small units are what let a contributor pick a piece up and deploy it into a training, a bill analysis or a policy review.

4.2 Required fields on every unit
Field	Purpose
Identifier	Stable, never reused
Type	One of the types above
Title and summary	Plain-language, consumer-facing
Body	Structured content, sectioned
Owner	Accountable contributor
Lifecycle status	Draft, in review, published, retired
Review date	When the content must next be reviewed
Citations	Sources, with enough detail to verify
Accessibility metadata	Reading level, alternative text, media requirements
Audience	Which roles or program types the unit addresses
4.3 Versions and provenance
Publishing a unit creates an immutable version with a version identifier, publish timestamp, author and approver.
Edits to a published unit create a new draft version; the published version remains live until the new one is approved.
Retiring a unit does not delete it. Retired versions remain resolvable by identifier for audit and citation.
The full history of every unit is retained and viewable by contributors.
4.4 Mandated instruments as first-class content
The DHS Equity Policy already requires two structured instruments: the Equity Analysis (eight steps: desired results, data, engagement, benefits and burdens, impact statement, accountability, alignment, sustainability) for actions with long-term impact requiring leadership approval, and the Equity Scan (six questions) for re-reviews and shortened timelines.

These are modelled as practice guides with the instrument built in as a working tool, not linked as a PDF. They are among the first units loaded in step 4 of the build sequence, because they are the most concrete, already-mandated piece of everyday work the system supports.

4.5 Policy orientation
The existing 47-minute audio orientation to the Equity Policy, the Equity Analysis Toolkit and DEI fundamentals is retained. Its home is a dedicated page in the Orientation hub, with transcript, chapter markers (policy, definitions, the eight-step analysis, the scan) and links from the transcript into the toolkit practice guide and the policy source. The toolkit practice guide links back to it. The home page carries a single pointer to it under "Start here" rather than the full player.

5. Program overlays
5.1 Definition
An overlay attaches to a content unit for a specific program (or division). It supplements or specialises the core for that program's staff. A consumer in that program sees one blended result; the seam is invisible.

5.2 Field-level rules
Every field on a content unit carries one of three overlay permissions:

Permission	Meaning	Examples
Supplement	Overlay may add to the core; core content is retained	Examples, program-specific scenarios, local contacts, related tools
Replace	Overlay may substitute its own content for the core field	Program-specific procedure steps, applicable forms
Protected	Overlay may never alter the field	Legal requirements, canonical definitions, accessibility standards, enterprise policy statements, citations to core sources
The protected-field list is owned by the administrator and approvers, versioned, and changeable only through the approval workflow.

5.3 Resolution
Resolution happens server-side at read time: fetch the core version, apply the program's published overlay version if one exists, return one object.
Resolution is deterministic. The same core version, overlay version and protected-field list always produce the same result.
Every resolved result carries provenance: core version identifier, overlay version identifier (or none), protected-field list version, resolution timestamp. Ordinary consumers see a seamless page; the provenance is available to contributors and in exports.
Where a program has no overlay, the core renders complete. There is no visual or functional indication that anything is missing.
5.4 Overlay lifecycle
Overlays are content. They carry the same owner, lifecycle status, review date, versioning and approval requirements as core units.

6. Situation index
6.1 Purpose
The situation index maps real circumstances a staff member may be in to the content units that help. It is the consumer's primary entry point and is deliberately decoupled from the content taxonomy, so contributors can reorganise concepts without breaking how people find things.

6.2 Situations are governed content
Each situation record has:

A plain-language name and aliases (the words staff actually use).
Audience (roles, program types).
Owner, lifecycle status and review date.
Relationships to other situations (broader, narrower, related, "often precedes").
Mappings to content units, many-to-many, with an ordering for presentation.
6.3 Search analytics
Consumer search behaviour (queries, zero-result searches, click-through) is captured to improve the situation index — surfacing missing aliases and missing situations. Analytics inform contributors; they never silently change canonical content or the index.

7. Accessibility requirements
The consumer and contributor interfaces meet WCAG 2.2 AA as an acceptance criterion for every feature, verified before deployment.
The content schema requires accessibility metadata on every unit (section 4.2).
Authoring validation blocks publication of units that fail baseline checks (missing alternative text, heading structure, reading-level flags, inaccessible attachments).
Program-specific accessibility guidance may be overlaid; baseline accessibility standards are protected fields.
Disability Services is the first program overlay and the first accessibility review partner.
8. Authorization, governance and audit
Row-level security in the database is required but not sufficient. All authorization decisions are enforced server-side in application code; the database policies are a second layer.
Draft and published records are separated. Consumer-facing queries can only reach published versions.
An approval workflow governs publication: draft → in review → published, with approver identity recorded on every transition.
An append-only audit log records every create, edit, transition, publish, retire and overlay action with actor, timestamp and before/after version identifiers.
Permission tests include negative cases: a consumer cannot read drafts, a contributor cannot publish, a contributor for one program cannot edit another program's overlays.
Contributor access is through the authoring interface only. Direct database access for contributors is not permitted; a minimal governed authoring form is a build-sequence requirement, not a later enhancement.
9. Stack and implementation constraints
Concern	Decision	Constraint
Framework	Next.js on Vercel	Retained from the previous build; production build must pass locally before any deploy
Database	PostgreSQL	The durable foundation. Schema, versioning and resolution logic belong to the application, not the provider
Platform	Supabase (Postgres, auth, row-level security)	An implementation choice, not an architectural dependency. Authentication and the resolution query sit behind a thin internal interface so the provider can be replaced or agency SSO integrated without rebuilding the content system. Do not build a general portability framework in version 1
Authentication	Role-based (consumer, contributor, approver, administrator)	Agency single sign-on is a target, not a version-1 blocker
Environments	Local, preview, production	Separate databases and secrets; health-check endpoint in every environment
10. Build sequence
Each step is complete only when it is deployed and verified.

Define invariants — ownership, lifecycle states, protected-field list, version-resolution rules. Timeboxed: one to two pages, not a governance programme. The purpose is to fix the rules the schema must honour before the schema exists.
Deploy the empty application — with health checks and environment separation. First green production deploy within the first working session.
Core content model — units, immutable versions, citations, audit provenance.
Load 10–20 representative real units — including the Equity Analysis and Equity Scan practice guides (section 4.4) and deliberately including difficult and conflicting examples, to expose schema assumptions early.
Situation index and situation-first discovery — accessible search and browse.
Disability Services overlays — prove deterministic blending, fallback to core, and protected-field behaviour.
Minimal governed authoring and approval workflow — enough for contributors to work without database access.
Test — permissions (including negative cases), accessibility, search quality, rollback, version traceability.
Migrate legacy content — inventory, map, transform, validate, load.
11. Existing build and migration
The existing application (one-dhs-equity-impact on Vercel) has a sound information architecture — situation-first entry, program hubs, work map, program guide, resource library, community briefs, cultural calendar, guided workflows — and substantial content (74 program records, 72 role records, 33 official sources, 18 resources). This is carried forward.
What it lacks is the data layer: all state is browser-local, with no database, accounts, authoring, versions or sharing. The rebuild is of the spine beneath the interface — PostgreSQL, versions, overlays, authoring and roles — with the existing front end and content migrated onto it.
Content inventory begins immediately and in parallel with steps 1–3: classify every existing piece by proposed type, note content that fits no type, and note where the schema's assumptions do not hold.
Migration itself is the last step (step 9), performed only once the content model has been proven with real units and overlays.
12. Out of scope for version 1
Agency single sign-on (target for version 2).
Overlays for programs beyond Disability Services (the model is proven on one program first).
Polished contributor authoring experience (the minimal governed form is in scope; refinement is not).
Analytics dashboards beyond what is needed to improve the situation index.
Automated content recommendations.
Integrations with other agency systems.
13. Open questions
Which fields are protected, replaceable and supplementable per content type — to be fixed in step 1.
The initial set of situations and their owners.
Review cadence per content type.
Which 10–20 units form the representative set in step 4.
